analysis.one_liner: Replaces the federal income tax with a flat tax on wages and business income and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The flat tax bill was referred to three House committees in March 1997 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would scrap the current income tax system and replace it with a single flat rate — 20%, dropping to 17% — applied only to wages, retirement payouts, and unemployment checks, with a large standard deduction. Interest, dividends, capital gains, and inherited wealth would not be taxed at all, and the estate tax would be repealed. It would also end most tax credits, rewrite pension rules, cap total federal spending through 2002 with automatic across-the-board cuts if Congress overspends, and require three-fifths of Congress to approve any future tax increase.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households with investment income (interest, dividends, and capital gains would go untaxed), heirs of large estates (estate tax repealed), and businesses (the corporate income tax replaced with a 20% falling to 17% tax, with pension rules loosened). Middle-income wage earners who don't itemize would also see simpler returns and, depending on their situation, lower bills.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the graduated income tax with one flat rate of 20%, dropping to 17% after 1998, applied to a tax base that only includes wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation.
Sets a large standard deduction — $22,000 for couples, $11,000 for singles, plus $5,000 per dependent — so households earning below those amounts would owe no income tax.
Repeals the alternative minimum tax, all tax credits, and the estate and gift taxes.
Simplifies the tax code dramatically and would make it harder to raise taxes in the future, requiring a three-fifths vote of each chamber for any income tax rate increase or new deduction.
Caps total federal spending at set dollar amounts for 1998 through 2002, enforced by automatic across-the-board cuts if Congress exceeds the cap.

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, the burden would shift toward wage earners: low-income working families would lose the tax credits repealed by the bill (the credit-repeal section covers the part of the tax code containing the Earned Income Tax Credit), while income from wealth would go untaxed. Federal programs would face hard spending caps with automatic cuts split 20% from defense and 80% from everything else.

drawbacks.text: Repeals all tax credits, which includes the Earned Income Tax Credit that supplements wages for low-income working families — a significant loss for households the flat rate alone may not offset.

Taxes only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation, leaving interest, dividends, and capital gains untaxed — a change that disproportionately benefits households whose income comes from wealth.
Repeals the estate and gift taxes retroactive to deaths after December 31, 1996, removing the tax on the largest inheritances entirely.

Repeals pension nondiscrimination rules and contribution limits, which currently prevent plans from being tilted toward a company's highest-paid executives, and removes the penalty on employers who pull excess assets out of pension plans.

Employee benefits like employer-provided health insurance would no longer be deductible business expenses, and workers for governments and tax-exempt organizations would face an explicit 20% tax on noncash compensation — raising the effective cost of health benefits for millions of workers.
Hard spending caps enforced by automatic sequestration (directed 20% at defense and 80% at non-defense programs) would force abrupt cuts to discretionary programs if spending exceeded the limits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers real simplification and a lower headline rate, and its large standard deduction would remove many low- and middle-income households from the tax rolls. But the design shifts the tax base almost entirely onto wages: income from investments and estates becomes tax-free, working families lose the Earned Income Tax Credit, and the pension-rule repeals most benefit plans covering executives and high earners. The distributional trade-off — cutting taxes on wealth while relying on wage taxation and spending caps — is the central cost an honest supporter would have to defend.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Ways and Means, Rules, and Budget committees on the day it was introduced, and nothing further ever happened to it before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dick Armey introduced the Freedom and Fairness Restoration Act of 1997 on March 12, 1997.
It was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee, and additionally to the Rules and Budget Committees.
The action history shows no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action of any kind after the referrals.
Ten members cosponsored the bill — 9 Republicans and 1 Democrat.
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: the existing tax code stayed in place. Low-income working families kept the Earned Income Tax Credit and other credits, and no industry or wealthy household secured the repeal of taxes on capital income and estates. Supporters gained nothing; opponents of the flat tax never even had to vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo — credits kept, taxes unchanged

for.name: Rep. Dick Armey
for.role: House Majority Leader and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the flat tax and spending-cap bill on March 12, 1997.

against.name: Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or hearing; it sat in his committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 9 Republican cosponsors came from the majority party, joined by a single Democrat; the bill never advanced far enough for a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would remove all tax on interest, dividends, capital gains, and inheritances, concentrating its rate cuts on income from wealth while keeping the tax base on wages. That gain comes at the expense of wage earners and federal revenue.

The 35% corporate income tax would be replaced with a 20% tax falling to 17%, and pension nondiscrimination rules and contribution limits would be repealed — but employer-paid fringe benefits like health insurance would lose their deduction.

Fringe benefits paid to employees would no longer be deductible for businesses, and a new 20% tax would apply to noncash compensation at government and tax-exempt employers — raising the cost of employer health coverage and encouraging employers to cut it.

Repealing nondiscrimination, participation, and distribution rules would free employers to design plans tilted toward top earners and to withdraw excess pension assets, while workers in those plans would lose protections that guarantee broad coverage.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: A tax form reduced to wages minus a standard deduction times one rate would sharply reduce demand for professional tax preparation, which is a cost of the simplification ordinary filers would otherwise benefit from.
